/usr/share/doc can have a ton of documentation, guides, handbooks, faqs, and howtos. Slackware has a very impressive set of docs in there while Arch Linux generally doesn't install the *-doc packages by default.

For example, this gem from Slackware's /usr/share/doc/Linux-FAQs/Linux-FAQ/Linux-FAQ

Q: How Does One Pronounce Linux?

A: This question produces an outrageous amount of heated debate.

If you want to hear Linus himself say how he pronounces it, download english.au or swedish.au from ftp://ftp.funet.fi/pub/Linux/PEOPLE/Linus/SillySounds/ If you have a sound card or the PC-speaker audio driver you can hear them by typing

$ cat english.au >/dev/audio

The difference isn't in the pronunciation of Linux but in the language Linus uses to say, "hello".

For the benefit of those who don't have the equipment or inclination: Linus pronounces Linux approximately as Leenus, where the ee is pronounced as in "feet," but rather shorter, and the u is like a much shorter version of the French eu sound in peur (pronouncing it as the u in "put" is probably passable).

The documentation isn't exactly very recent, though, that FAQ is no exception. You would most likely need to do a sudo modprobe snd-pcm-oss to get /dev/audio, /dev/dsp and stuff working.

My advice: If you use a command a lot or you have trouble remembering it (or both, as is often the case for newbies and package managers), an alias may help. Aliases automatically convert a command into another command. There are a lot of places you can store them but I prefer ~/.bashrc (if you don't use bash, there's probably a similar nomenclature for your file). It's a hidden file (hence the . in front of it) so it may not appear in your GUI file manager (typically Ctrl+H toggles hidden files).

Pick a spot somewhere (the end is probably the best idea) and follow the syntax:

[alias] = '[command]'

Here's some examples I use very often to simplify the use of my package manager.

alias xinstall='sudo xbps-install -S'
alias xsearch='xbps-query -Rs'
alias xremove='sudo xbps-remove -R'

If you're feeling confident, you can look into making functions. This lets you do some things you can't with an alias, like inserting things in the middle of the alias or using loops. Here's one I use for converting to .webm format. (Warning: It's not pretty but it works just fine.)

function webmadv {
 echo "Filename: "
 read inputfile
 inputtooutput='.webm'
 outputfile=$inputfile$inputtooutput
 echo "Start time: "
 read tstart
 echo "End time: "
 read tend
 echo "Resolution (vertical dimension): "
 read resolution
 echo "Quality (i.e. 500k, 1M): "
 read quality
 echo "CRF (0-51): "
 read constantratefactor
 ffmpeg -ss $tstart -i $inputfile -to $tend -vf scale=-1:$resolution -c:v libvpx -b:v $quality -c:a libvorbis -q:a 0 -crf $constantratefactor -threads 4 $outputfile
}

And while I can't go into detail, I also recommend looking into cron if you have stuff you want to schedule to repeat or do at certain times. It's a little more involved than the stuff I just mentioned so check out the Arch and Gentoo wikis for details.
